av_event.line_text: I do, mostly. I read a lot. Crime, mainly. I've got one on the go now, a Scottish detective series, and I'm on number six.
av_event.what: A young man in a dark hoodie, holding a mug, walks slowly across the background behind Alison, past the glass-fronted cabinet, and goes out of frame. Alison's eyes flick sideways towards him for a moment and then come back to the screen. She keeps talking without stopping.

text:
A: Hiya! Can you hear me?
B: Yes, I can. Hello. I'm Alison.
A: Neil. I'm in Shipley, near Bradford. Last one of the day for me, I think.
B: And me. I'm in Stockton-on-Tees.
A: Oh, Teesside! I've walked bits of the Cleveland Way, up past Saltburn. Lovely bit of coast, that.
B: It is. I don't get up there as much as I should. I mostly walk along the Tees of a morning, down by the Barrage.
A: Every morning?
B: Most. About forty minutes. There's a heron I've got quite attached to. I told someone earlier that I say good morning to it.
A: Ha, that's not daft at all. I talk to the sheep on Ilkley Moor. They don't answer either.
B: You walk a lot, then?
A: Most weekends. The Dales, the moors. I did the Coast to Coast a few years back, and that finishes at Robin Hood's Bay, so not far from you really. My knees still haven't forgiven me.
B: Goodness. That's a long way.
A: Two weeks, give or take. What did you do before, Alison? Or are you still working?
B: I'm retired. I was a medical secretary at a GP practice in Norton. Twenty-seven years.
A: Twenty-seven years. You'll have seen everything.
B: Erm, a fair bit. Mostly I was the one who knew where the files were. And which patients needed a gentler phone call.
A: That's the important job, though, isn't it? I'm a lab technician at the university in Bradford, and it's the same. Nobody notices you till summat goes missing.
B: That's exactly it.
A: Do you enjoy being retired? Our mam says the first year she didn't know what to do with herself.
B: I do, mostly. I read a lot. Crime, mainly. I've got one on the go now, a Scottish detective series, and I'm on number six.
A: Oh, which one?
B: Erm, I'd have to look. It's a library book. He's very miserable, the detective.
A: They always are! I read a lot of translated stuff, Italian, Scandinavian. Same rule. Nobody's happy in Swedish crime.
B: No. I suppose that's half the appeal.
A: Do you live on your own, or...?
B: My son's back with me at the moment. He's thirty-one and works shifts at a warehouse. So tea's either half five or whenever he gets in.
A: Ha, I'm the reverse. I'm forty-nine and I live with me mam and dad. I moved back when me dad's mobility got bad, and sort of never left. So I do the tea and they tell me it needs more salt.
B: I think that's lovely, actually. That you're there for them.
A: Well, it works both ways. Our mam still does me washing, so I'm not complaining.
B: My mam would have liked that. Someone being around. She died in 2016.
A: Oh, I'm sorry. That's not that long ago, is it?
B: No. It was a long illness, so. Erm, do you go to church at all? Sorry, that's a strange question.
A: Not strange at all. Methodist chapel, most Sundays. Partly for me mam, partly for the singing. I'm in a choir as well, bass.
B: I go to the parish church. I help with the coffee morning. I always do a lemon drizzle.
A: Now you're talking. If you ever want a taster up in Shipley, I'm
